title: Question 1
stem:
The Earth may be considered as a uniform sphere of radius $6.37 \times 10^6\text{m}$.

Cambridge is at a point on the Earth's surface that has a latitude of $52.2^{\circ}$ north of the Equator, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

{{figure:figure_1_1}}

Fig. 1.1

As the Earth spins on its axis, Cambridge moves in a circle that is parallel to the Equator but with a smaller radius.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Show that the radius of the circle around which Cambridge moves is $3.90 \times 10^6\text{m}$.
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 1.1 and think about which circle Cambridge actually travels on. It is not the full Earth radius, but the horizontal distance from the rotation axis to Cambridge.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the small circle Cambridge moves on**
Think of yourself standing in Cambridge as Earth spins. You go round the North-South axis once per day. The centre of your circle is on that axis, not at the centre of Earth. So your orbital radius is the horizontal side of the right-angled triangle in Fig. 1.1.

Step 2: **Use cosine to find the adjacent side**
The hypotenuse is the Earth radius $R = 6.37 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$ and the angle to the Equator is $52.2^{\circ}$. The adjacent horizontal side is: $$r = R \cos 52.2^{\circ}$$ $$r = 6.37 \times 10^6 \times \cos 52.2^{\circ} = 3.90 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$$ That shows the required result.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the speed at which Cambridge moves around the circle.

markscheme_points.text: v = 2πr / T or v = rω and ω = 2π / T

hints: Hint 1: Speed means distance travelled divided by time taken. What distance does Cambridge travel in one full spin, and how long does one full spin of Earth take?
Hint 2: Recall how circumference links to radius, and remember to convert the period from hours or days into seconds for SI units.
Hint 3: Combine $v = 2\pi r / T$ with $r = 3.90 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$ and $T = 24 \times 60 \times 60 \text{ s}$ to calculate $v$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Get the time for one rotation**
Earth spins once in one day. That is: $$T = 24 \text{ hours} = 24 \times 60 \times 60 = 86400 \text{ s}$$ A common slip is to leave $T$ in hours. For speed in $\text{m s}^{-1}$ you must use seconds.

Step 2: **Get the distance for one rotation**
In time $T$, Cambridge travels one circumference of its small circle: $$\text{distance} = 2\pi r$$ with $r = 3.90 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$ from (a)(i).

Step 3: **Calculate the speed**
Speed is distance over time: $$v = \frac{2\pi r}{T}$$ $$v = \frac{2\pi \times 3.90 \times 10^6}{86400} = 2.8 \times 10^2 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$ So about $280 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ eastwards. This is slower than at the Equator because $r$ is smaller.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: A student of mass $58.6\text{kg}$ stands on horizontal ground in Cambridge.
parts.text: Determine the magnitude of the resultant force that acts to cause the circular motion of the student.
hints: Hint 1: The student is moving in a circle at constant speed, so there must be a net inward force providing the centripetal acceleration. Which quantities do you now know: mass, speed and circle radius?
Hint 2: Think about the standard centripetal force relation linking $m$, $v$ and $r$, then substitute $m = 58.6 \text{ kg}$, $v \approx 280 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $r = 3.90 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the centripetal force law**
Uniform circular motion needs a resultant force toward the centre of the circle: $$F = \frac{mv^2}{r}$$ Here $m = 58.6 \text{ kg}$, $v$ is your answer from (a)(ii), and $r = 3.90 \times 10^6 \text{ m}$ is the radius of Cambridge's circle, not the full Earth radius.

Step 2: **Substitute and evaluate**
$$F = \frac{58.6 \times (280)^2}{3.90 \times 10^6}$$ $$F \approx 1.2 \text{ N}$$ This is tiny compared to the weight of about $570 \text{ N}$, but it is the small net inward force needed to keep the student circling with Earth.

markscheme_points.text: arrow pointing horizontally to the left

hints: Hint 1: For any circular motion the resultant force points to the centre of that circle. Where is the centre of Cambridge's circular path in Fig. 1.2?
parts.proper_answer: Arrow drawn from the student horizontally to the left, toward the Earth's rotation axis (the centre of Cambridge's circle).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Point to the centre of the motion**
The student circles around the Earth's axis with the circle parallel to the Equator. So the centre of the circle lies horizontally inward from Cambridge, on the axis. The resultant (centripetal) force must point exactly there. On Fig. 1.2 that is a horizontal arrow to the left starting at the student.

parts.label: (b)(iii)

markscheme_points.text: arrow from student pointing along the dotted line, labelled ‘weight’
upwards arrow from student pointing in a direction to the left of normal and above the tangent to the Earth, labelled ‘contact force’

hints: Hint 1: Only two real forces act on the standing student: gravity and the push from the ground. Think about the true direction of each if Earth were not rotating.

Hint 2: The vector sum of those two forces must equal the horizontal resultant from (b)(ii). If weight acts straight to Earth's centre along the dotted line, which way must the contact force tilt so the sum points horizontally left?
parts.proper_answer: Weight arrow from student along dotted line toward centre of Earth, labelled weight. Contact force arrow from student directed upwards and tilted to the left of the normal, labelled contact force, such that weight + contact force = horizontal resultant to left.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Draw the weight**
Gravity always pulls toward the centre of Earth. On Fig. 1.3 that is straight down along the dotted line from the student toward the centre. Draw an arrow that way and label it weight.

Step 2: **Draw the contact force tilted to give the correct resultant**
The ground pushes back with a contact force (normal plus friction combined). If it were exactly opposite to weight, the resultant would be zero. To leave a small net force horizontally to the left, the contact force must point generally upward but tilted slightly to the left of the normal, i.e. above the tangent and to the left. Draw that upward tilted arrow from the student and label it contact force. Added as vectors, weight plus this contact force gives the horizontal leftward resultant.
